The trailer stays in your history after you push, and you can delete the line before committing if you do not want the commit linked.Remote URL redaction in logs.
L74: When a fetch or push fails, error messages and `.entire/logs/` entries strip REDACTEDwords from URLs, for example `https://user:****@github.com`, so credentials stay out of local log files.
L75: What Redaction Covers
L76: 
L77: Redaction covers the content Entire writes into checkpoint storage. It does not cover everything Entire touches.
L78: Content  | Written to  | Redaction applied  | Reaches a remote
L79: --- | --- | --- | ---
L80: Prompts and transcripts (`prompt.txt`, `full.jsonl`, `transcript.jsonl`)  | Checkpoint storage  | Layers 1 through 8, plus the OpenAI Privacy Filter at push time on the branch backend  | Yes, on push
L81: Checkpoint metadata (`metadata.json`, `checkpoint.json`)  | Checkpoint storage  | Layers 1 through 8. The structural-field skip rules exempt file paths and ID fields, so `files_touched` paths are stored as written  | Yes, on push
L82: Externalized image assets (`assets/`)  | Checkpoint storage  | None. Every layer skips the assets subtree  | Yes, on push, when `redaction.externalize_images` is on
L83: Inline base64 images left in a transcript  | Checkpoint storage  | None. The JSONL skip rules exclude objects whose `type` starts with `image` or equals `base64`  | Yes, on push
L84: Source-file snapshots  | Shadow branch  | None. Raw working-tree blobs, minus gitignored paths  | No, unless you push the shadow branch yourself
L85: Raw agent session files, for example `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/*.jsonl`  | Your agent’s own directory  | None. Entire reads these files and does not rewrite them, because the agent is writing to them concurrently  | No
L86: Diagnostic logs (`.entire/logs/entire.log`)  | Local, gitignored  | Not redacted, but the CLI logs metadata only (IDs, ref names, counts, and timings) and strips REDACTEDwords from remote URLs  | No
L87: `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer  | Your own commits  | Not applicable. The value is an ID  | Yes, on push
L88: Redaction Layers
L89: 
L90: Nine layers run in this order. Layers 1 through 8 use regexes, entropy scoring, or structural validation during condensation. Layer 9 calls a local model at push time.
L91: 
L92: CLI 0.10.2 uses Betterleaks for layer 2. Scanner selection first appears in `v0.10.3-nightly.202608210613.680d64782`.
L93: #  | Layer  | Runs  | Replacement
L94: --- | --- | --- | ---
L95: 1  | Entropy scoring. Alphanumeric runs of 10 or more characters whose Shannon entropy exceeds 4.5  | On every write  | `REDACTED`
L96: 2  | Secret pattern matching. Entire runs one or both configured scanner engines: 【15†Betterleaks†github.com】, which covers several hundred known secret formats, and 【16†goredact†github.com】, which validates a smaller set of provider and contextual token shapes  | On every write, with at least one scanner enabled  | `REDACTED`
L97: 3  | Provider token prefixes. Deterministic prefix rules for low-entropy credential formats the first two layers miss in isolation, such as Supabase `sb_secret_` and `sbp_`  | On every write  | `REDACTED`
L98: 4  | Credentialed URIs. URLs embedding a REDACTEDword, such as `REDACTED` or `REDACTED`, redacted as a unit  | On every write  | `REDACTED`
L99: 5  | Database connection strings. JDBC URIs, database URLs, Postgres keyword DSNs, and semicolon-delimited connection strings. A string with a real REDACTEDword is redacted whole, because a partial fragment can still expose sensitive material  | On every write  | `REDACTED`
L100: 6  | User-defined rules. Your inline rules and rule packs  | When configured  | `REDACTED`
L101: 7  | Bounded credential values. Assignments whose key names a credential, such as `DB_PASSWORD` or `PGPASSWORD`. Inside JSON, a generic `REDACTEDword` key is redacted when the surrounding object also carries a host-like and a user-like field. The key survives; the value does not  | On every write  | `REDACTED`
L102: 8  | PII detection. Email, phone, and US street address  | When configured  | `[REDACTED_EMAIL]` and similar
L103: 9  | OpenAI Privacy Filter. A token-classification model that catches names and other personal data regex misses  | When configured, at push time, on the branch backend  | Category tokens
L104: Layers 1, 3, 4, 5, and 7 run on every checkpoint write and have no setting that turns them off. Layer 2 always runs at least one scanner. Layers 6, 8, and 9 run only when you configure them.Secret scanner engines. Betterleaks runs by default and provides broader format coverage. goredact is off by default and uses validators such as token length or checksum checks to improve precision. You can run either engine or both.Entire reads scanner selection only from the committed `.entire/settings.json` file.
L105: It ignores scanner keys in `.entire/settings.local.json` and logs a warning because scanner choice changes the checkpoint content shared with everyone who reads the repository history.Entire refuses to load settings when both scanners are off. If goredact is the only active scanner and it fails during a scan, Entire stops the checkpoint write. If Betterleaks is also active, Entire completes the write with Betterleaks coverage. See 【17†Secret Scanner Engines】 for configuration.Avoiding over-redaction.
L106: Entire skips fields where a match is more likely to be noise than a secret: fields named `signature`, keys ending in `id` or `ids`, structural path fields (`filepath`, `file_path`, `cwd`, `root`, `directory`, `dir`, and `path`), and objects whose `type` starts with `image` or equals `base64`.It also leaves placeholders alone.
L107: Entire matches placeholders exactly (`changeme`, `example`, `placeholder`, `your_REDACTEDword`, `your_secret`, and prior `REDACTED` markers) and by shape: shell expansions such as `${DB_PASSWORD}`, bracketed names such as `<REDACTEDword>`, and mask runs of three or more `*`, `x`, `.`, or `-`. A connection string whose REDACTEDword is a placeholder survives intact.These skips trade detection coverage for a lower false-positive rate. A secret parked in a `path` field or inside a base64 blob is not redacted.
L108: User-Defined Redaction
L109: 
L110: User-defined rules add a regex layer for strings the built-in detectors do not know: internal token formats, project codenames, customer names, or any other pattern you would rather keep out of session archives.Rules use 【18†Go RE2 syntax†pkg.go.dev】, so lookarounds and backreferences are unavailable. Matches become the bare `REDACTED` token. Labels serve diagnostics only.You can supply rules two ways, both configured in 【19†Privacy and Redaction】:
L111:   * Inline rules under `redaction.custom_redactions`, for a handful of patterns.
L112:   * Rule packs, YAML or JSON files under `.entire/redactors/`, for reusable sets. A pack declares `name` matching its filename stem, a `version`, and one or more `rules`, each with an `id` and a `regex`.
L113: Self-tests. A rule may declare `samples` with `{ input, redacted }` expectations. Entire checks them when it loads the pack and logs a warning on a mismatch, which catches typos without disabling the rule. Entire logs an invalid regex and skips that rule rather than crashing the redactor.When rules take effect. On the next CLI or hook invocation. No reload command exists.Personal rules.
L114: Put packs you do not want to share under `.entire/redactors/local/`, which `entire enable` keeps gitignored, so a codename or a customer reference does not become shared repository configuration.
L115: PII Redaction (Optional)
L116: 
L117: PII redaction runs as layer 8, in addition to secret detection. It is off by default.
L118: 
L119: Category  | Default once PII is enabled  | Replacement
L120: --- | --- | ---
L121: `email`  | On  | `[REDACTED_EMAIL]`
L122: `phone`  | On  | `[REDACTED_PHONE]`
L123: `address` (US street addresses)  | Off, because it produces more false positives  | `[REDACTED_ADDRESS]`
L124: Email allowlist. Bot and CI addresses stay readable, because they appear in nearly every transcript and identify no one: `noreply@*`, `actions@*`, `*@users.noreply.github.com`, and `*@noreply.github.com`.Custom patterns. You can add your own patterns under `custom_patterns`, where the label becomes part of the token. A pattern named `employee_id` produces `[REDACTED_EMPLOYEE_ID]`.A custom pattern that reveals an internal ID format is itself sensitive.
L125: Put those in `.entire/settings.local.json`, which stays out of Git, rather than in the committed `.entire/settings.json`. See 【20†PII redaction】 for the settings.
L126: OpenAI Privacy Filter (Optional)
L127: 
L128: The 【21†OpenAI Privacy Filter†github.com】 (`opf`) is a 1.5B-parameter token-classification model that finds names, addresses, account numbers, and other personal data the regex layers miss. It runs as layer 9, and it is off by default.
L129: OPF applies to the branch backend. The pre-push rewrite operates on `entire/checkpoints/v1`. Repositories on the ref-based backend, which is the default for repositories enabled with CLI 0.10.0 or later, push checkpoints without the OPF REDACTED. Check `checkpoints.primary.type` before relying on OPF.
L130: When it runs. OPF runs at push time, not at commit time. Local commits stay on the eight regex layers, so per-commit latency is unchanged. During `git push`, the pre-push hook re-reads each unpushed checkpoint commit, runs the model over its content, and writes new commits carrying an `Entire-OPF-Applied: true` trailer. The local ref fast-forwards to the rewritten tip, and those commits are what reach the remote. The original commits become unreachable and are swept by `git gc`.Two consequences follow.
L131: The remote sees only OPF-redacted content once OPF is enabled, and local-only commits carry eight-layer redaction until the moment you push. If you never push, OPF never runs.The pre-push prompt. When OPF is enabled and your terminal is interactive, the hook asks before running:
L132: 
L133:     `Run OpenAI Privacy Filter on these checkpoints?
L134:     Adds ~30s but redacts names/PII the regex layers can't catch.
L135:     Ctrl-C to cancel the push.
L136: 
L137:       > Yes     run OPF this push
L138:         No      skip OPF, push as-is
L139:         Always  run OPF on every push from now on
L140:     `
L141: Yes runs OPF for this push. No skips it, and the eight-layer content reaches the remote. Always runs OPF and writes `prompt_default: "always"` to `.entire/settings.local.json` so later pushes stop asking. Ctrl-C aborts the push, and no refs reach the remote.Without a TTY, which covers CI and scripted pushes, Entire skips the prompt and runs OPF, printing a progress line to stderr so the wait is visible.The `ENTIRE_OPF` override. `ENTIRE_OPF` beats both the setting and the prompt, for a single push.
L142: The decision resolves in this order: `ENTIRE_OPF`, then `prompt_default` in settings, then the prompt, then the non-interactive default of running.
L143: 
L144:     `ENTIRE_OPF=no git push
L145:     `
L146: `ENTIRE_OPF=no` skips OPF for that push. `ENTIRE_OPF=yes` runs it without asking. Use `no` when CI pushes from a machine with no `opf` installed, or for a one-off push while you fix a broken install.Failures abort the push. If `opf` is missing from `$PATH`, fails to start, or times out, the rewrite aborts the push with `OPF runtime failed; aborting push`. Nothing reaches the remote.
L147: Enabling OPF states that you do not want unredacted content leaving the machine, so falling back to eight-layer redaction silently would break that contract.Enabling OPF with no category selected fails the same way. Entire cannot tag commits as OPF-applied without a scan, so the push aborts with a configuration error instead. Enable a category, set `enabled: false`, or REDACTED `ENTIRE_OPF=no`.The rewrite also refuses to run when it would rewrite history it does not own.
L148: It aborts if local checkpoints have diverged from the remote, if a first push exceeds the bootstrap commit cap, if the batch exceeds the inference byte cap, or if another worktree moves the ref mid-rewrite. See 【22†OpenAI Privacy Filter】 for the caps and their overrides.`command` is local-only, and the file must be untracked. `command` names the binary Entire executes during `git push`, so whoever controls that string controls what runs on your machine. Entire honors it only when it is genuinely yours:
L149:   1. It has to come from `.entire/settings.local.json`, not the committed `.entire/settings.json`.
L150:   2. That file has to be untracked, meaning absent from both the Git index and `HEAD`.
L151: The second check carries the weight. A filename proves nothing on its own, because `.gitignore` does not apply to an already-tracked path: `git add -f .entire/settings.local.json` commits the file, and a fresh clone materializes it with the committed content. A pull request that pairs a `command` with a payload would then execute on every machine that checks the branch out, and a JSON settings diff does not read as executable to a reviewer.The rule covers the whole file.

L18: # About setup types for code scanning
L19: 
L20: Depending on your needs, GitHub offers a default or advanced setup for code scanning.
L21: 
L22: Copy markdown
L23: 
L24: ## In this article
L25: 
L26:   * 【4†About default setup】
L27: 
L28:   * 【5†Customization of default setup】

L30:   * 【6†About advanced setup】

L33: ## 【4†About default setup】
L34: 
L35: Default setup for code scanning is the quickest, easiest, most low-maintenance way to enable code scanning for your repository. Based on the code in your repository, default setup will automatically create a custom code scanning configuration. You can also customize this configuration, including at scale across your organization, without creating or maintaining a workflow file. See 【5†Customization of default setup】.
L36: With default setup, the code written in CodeQL-supported languages in your repository will be scanned using CodeQL:
L37:   * When you enable it.
L38:   * On each push to the repository's default branch, or any protected branch. For more information on protected branches, see 【8†About protected branches】.
L39:   * When creating or committing to a pull request based against the repository's default branch, or any protected branch, excluding pull requests from forks.
L40:   * On a weekly schedule, if a push or pull request has triggered a scan in the last 180 days.
L41:   * Every 30 days for inactive repositories, when enabled by an organization owner. See 【9†Configuring global security settings for your organization】.
L42: Weekly scheduled scans start only after a push or pull request triggers a scan with default setup enabled. The initial scan and scans triggered by configuration or language changes do not start or extend the weekly schedule. Pushes and pull requests from before default setup was enabled do not count.
L43: ### 【10†Supported languages】
L44: We recommend enabling default setup for eligible repositories if there is any chance the repositories will include at least one CodeQL-supported language in the future. If you enable default setup on a repository that does not include any CodeQL-supported languages, default setup will not run any scans or use any GitHub Actions minutes.
L45: If CodeQL-supported languages are added to the repository's default branch, default setup will automatically begin scanning CodeQL-supported languages and using GitHub Actions minutes. For more information on CodeQL-supported languages, see 【11†Code scanning with CodeQL】.
L46: If the code in a repository changes to include any CodeQL-supported languages, GitHub will automatically update the code scanning configuration to include the new language. If code scanning fails with the new configuration, GitHub will resume the previous configuration automatically so the repository does not lose code scanning coverage.
L47: ## 【5†Customization of default setup】
L48: 
L49: After running an initial analysis of your code with default setup, you can make changes to your configuration to better meet your needs.
L50: ### 【12†Configuration options】
L51: 
L52: For existing configurations of default setup, you can edit:
L53:   * Which languages default setup will analyze.
L54:   * The query suite run during analysis. For more information on the available query suites, see 【13†CodeQL query suites】.
L55:   * The threat models (public preview) to use for analysis. Your choice of threat model determines which sources of tainted data are treated as a risk to your application. During the public preview, threat models are supported only for analysis of Java/Kotlin and C#. For more information about threat models, see 【14†Including local sources of tainted data in default setup】.
L56: If your codebase depends on a library or framework that is not recognized by the standard libraries included with CodeQL, you can also extend the CodeQL coverage in default setup using CodeQL model packs. For more information, see 【15†Extending CodeQL coverage with CodeQL model packs in default setup】.
L57: You can also apply a custom CodeQL configuration file to default setup across your organization at once, or for a single repository, by setting the `github-codeql-config-file` repository property. A custom configuration file applied using the `github-codeql-config-file` property is merged with the configuration that code scanning default setup generates automatically.
L58: Code scanning default setup allows you to customize some analysis settings in the user interface, such as which threat models or CodeQL model packs to use. These selections are kept in the merged configuration: the threat models selected in the default setup UI are combined with any threat models specified in the configuration file, and model packs configured in the UI are kept.
L59: This lets you meet customization needs that previously required advanced setup, while keeping the low-maintenance benefits of default setup. See 【16†Repository properties for code scanning】 and 【17†Editing your configuration of default setup】.
L60: Additional configuration options that are shared between all code scanning setup types are available. See 【18†Repository properties for code scanning】.
L61: ### 【19†Available runners】
L62: 
L63: You can use default setup for all CodeQL-supported languages on self-hosted runners or GitHub-hosted runners.
L64: 
L65: You can assign self-hosted runners for default setup by giving the runners the default `code-scanning` label, or you can optionally give them custom labels so that individual repositories can use different runners.
L66: Unless you have a specific use case, we recommend that you only assign runners with the default `code-scanning` label. However, you may want to use custom labels to:
L67: 
L68:   * Assign more powerful self-hosted runners to critical repositories for faster code scanning analysis.
L69:   * Run your code scanning analyses on a particular platform (for example, macOS).
L70:   * Have granular control over the workload for your GitHub-hosted runners and self-hosted runners.
L71: ## 【6†About advanced setup】
L72: If the customization options available for default setup, including a custom configuration file, don't meet your needs, you should instead configure advanced setup. Advanced setup for code scanning is helpful when you need to define your own GitHub Actions workflow, for example to build compiled languages, use a matrix build, or change the analysis schedule. You can set up code scanning with GitHub Actions or an external continuous integration or continuous delivery/deployment (CI/CD) system.
L73: If you run code scanning using multiple configurations, an alert will sometimes have multiple analysis origins. If an alert has multiple analysis origins, you can view the status of the alert for each analysis origin on the alert page. For more information, see 【20†Code scanning alerts】.
L74: ### 【21†With GitHub Actions】
L75: 
L76: By creating and editing a GitHub Actions workflow file, you can define how to build compiled languages, choose which queries to run, select the languages to scan, use a matrix build, and more. You also have access to all the options for controlling workflows, for example: changing the scan schedule, defining workflow triggers, specifying specialist runners to use.
L77: ### 【22†With a third-party CI/CD system】
L78: 
L79: As an alternative to running code scanning within GitHub using GitHub Actions, you can analyze code in an external CI/CD system, then upload the results to GitHub.
L80: The CodeQL CLI is a standalone, command-line tool that you can use to analyze code. You can add the CodeQL CLI to your third-party system, or use another third-party static analysis tool that can produce results as Static Analysis Results Interchange Format (SARIF) 2.1.0 data. For more information, see 【23†CodeQL CLI】 and 【24†SARIF support for code scanning】.
L81: 
L82: Alerts for code scanning that you generate externally are displayed in the same way as those for code scanning that you generate within GitHub.
L83: ## 【7†Next steps】
L84: 
L85: You can enable default setup for a single repository, multiple repositories, or all repositories in an organization at the same time.
L86: 
L87:   * For a single repository, see 【25†Configuring default setup for code scanning】.
L88:   * For bulk enablement, see 【26†Configuring default setup for code scanning at scale】.
L89: 
L90: To configure advanced setup instead, see 【27†Configuring advanced setup for code scanning】.

L21: # Store Checkpoints in Another Repository
L22: 
L23: Push checkpoint history to a repository separate from your source code.
L24: 
L25: Copy page Copy page
L26: 
L27: Configure a 【9†checkpoint remote】 when checkpoint history should follow a different sharing boundary than your source code, such as keeping agent transcripts private for a public project. Your code continues to live in the main repository, and Entire pushes checkpoint data to the separate one.
L28: ## Configure the Checkpoint Remote
L29: 
L30: Create a separate, empty repository for checkpoint data, then run this from your project:
L31: 
L32:     `entire configure --checkpoint-remote github:owner/repo
L33:     `
L34: 
L35: The value uses the format `provider:owner/repo`, where the provider is `github` or `gitlab`. This writes:
L36: 
L37: .entire/settings.json
L38: 
L39:     `{
L40:       "strategy_options": {
L41:         "checkpoint_remote": {
L42:           "provider": "github",
L43:           "repo": "owner/repo"
L44:         }
L45:       }
L46:     }
L47:     `
L48: Commit and push `.entire/settings.json` when the checkpoint remote should apply to the whole project. That setting is what entire.com reads to locate checkpoint data.
L49: 
L50: If you mirror your code repository from GitHub, mirror the checkpoint repository too, in the same region. entire.com reads checkpoint data through that mirror, so without it the project shows no checkpoints even though your pushes succeed.
L51: ## Keep Checkpoints under the Same Owner
L52: Use a checkpoint repository with the same owner or organization as your code repository. Code at `github.com/acme/app` pairs with `github:acme/app-checkpoints`, because `acme` owns both. A committed `checkpoint_remote` is inherited by everyone who clones or forks the project.
L53: To keep a contributor’s session data out of the upstream project’s checkpoint repository, Entire ignores the setting when it looks inherited, and uploads checkpoints to the remote you push to instead, following the rules in 【10†Choose Where Checkpoints Are Uploaded】. `entire status` shows when and why the setting is ignored. Entire treats the setting as yours when either of these is true:
L54:   * It is in the gitignored `.entire/settings.local.json`.
L55:   * Your `origin` and every push URL of the remote you push to are owned by the same account or organization as the checkpoint repository.
L56: Requiring the push remote as well covers contributors who cloned the upstream repository and added their own fork, where `origin` belongs to the upstream project. If your checkpoint repository is owned by a different account or organization than your code, configure it in `.entire/settings.local.json` so it is always used:
L57: 
L58:     `entire configure --local --checkpoint-remote github:owner/repo
L59:     `
L60: ## Push Behavior
L61: When you push code, Entire pushes checkpoint data to the checkpoint repository separately, using the same protocol, SSH or HTTPS, as your Git remote. The checkpoint repository is used regardless of which of your remotes would otherwise receive checkpoints. If the checkpoint repository cannot be reached, your main Git push still succeeds. Entire keeps the checkpoint data locally and warns that it could not sync.
L62: With the legacy branch storage backend, Entire also fetches existing checkpoint data from the checkpoint repository once, if it has data you don’t. The default `git-refs` backend fetches checkpoints on demand instead.
L63: ## Use a Separate Token
L64: 
L65: Set `ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_TOKEN` to authenticate checkpoint fetches and pushes with a dedicated token, without changing the credentials for your code repository. When it is set, Entire:
L66:   * Adds the token to the HTTPS Git operations it runs for checkpoints.
L67:   * Rewrites SSH remotes, including `origin`, to the equivalent HTTPS URL for checkpoint operations, so the token can authenticate. If a URL cannot be rewritten, the operation runs over SSH without the token and Entire prints a warning.
L68:   * Without a `checkpoint_remote`, applies the token to the remote chosen as described in 【10†Choose Where Checkpoints Are Uploaded】.
L69: 
L70:     `ENTIRE_CHECKPOINT_TOKEN=<token> git push
L71:     `

L21: # Choose Where Checkpoints Are Uploaded
L22: 
L23: Control which remote receives checkpoint data when a repository has several.
L24: 
L25: Copy page Copy page
L26: 
L27: Entire uploads checkpoints to one place, the checkpoint destination. It is either:
L28:   * One of your existing remotes, chosen automatically or pinned with `--checkpoint-push-remote <remote-name>`. Checkpoints are uploaded when you run `git push` to that remote.
L29:   * A separate checkpoint repository, set with `--checkpoint-remote`. See 【9†Store Checkpoints in Another Repository】.
L30: The two flags differ by one word but mean different things: `--checkpoint-push-remote` picks which of your remotes receives checkpoints, while `--checkpoint-remote` sends them to a different repository altogether. `entire status` shows the current destination, where it came from, and how many checkpoints are unpushed. With the default `git-refs` 【10†storage backend】, `entire checkpoint list --outgoing` lists them. Every `entire enable` run ends by naming the destination.
L31: ## Which Remote Receives Checkpoints
L32: 
L33: If you push code to several remotes, checkpoints go to exactly one of them. Entire picks it in this order:
L34:   1. `strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote`, if set. If it names a remote that isn’t configured, checkpoints don’t sync.
L35:   2. The remote of your first push whose target matches the branch’s configured push destination. Entire announces the choice and keeps it.
L36:   3. `origin`
L37:   4. The sole remote, if the repository has exactly one
L38:   5. The first remote in `.git/config` order
L39: A push to any other remote carries no checkpoint data, unless every push URL of both remotes names the same GitHub repository. For example, `git@github.com:acme/widgets.git` and its Entire mirror `entire://<cluster>/gh/acme/widgets` reach the same repository, so a push to either carries the checkpoints.
L40: ## Choose the Remote
L41: When a repository has several remotes that could receive checkpoints, the first interactive `entire enable` asks which one to use, after agent selection and before any hooks or settings are written. Running `entire enable` again in an enabled repository does not ask again. Choosing a remote saves `strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote` in `.entire/settings.local.json`, so teammates do not inherit a remote name specific to your clone. Keeping the current destination writes nothing.
L42: To select a remote without the picker:
L43: 
L44:     `entire enable --yes --checkpoint-push-remote fork
L45:     `
L46: The remote must already exist. Use the same command to change the destination later, or to repair a saved selection that names a missing remote. An explicit flag pins the named remote, even if it is currently selected automatically. `--yes` alone does not change the destination. Selecting a destination does not re-enable disabled checkpoint pushing, upload existing checkpoints immediately, or move or delete checkpoint history on other remotes.
L47: ## Edge Cases
L48:   * An SSH host alias from `~/.ssh/config`, such as `git@github-work:acme/widgets.git`, counts as GitHub when Git runs plain `ssh`. With a custom `GIT_SSH_COMMAND` or `core.sshCommand`, the alias cannot be resolved, so it does not match.
L49:   * `entire enable` always says where checkpoints will be uploaded. When you chose the destination, it also says how. If a saved destination is unusable, it reports the problem instead of showing the privacy notice, unless checkpoints still upload to a dedicated checkpoint repository.
